contextHeader: Conversion — specific, first-person CTA microcopy

options.label: Specific first-person CTA copy ('Start my free trial')

claim: Bundling complementary products or plan features at a modest discount increases average order value more reliably than a flat sitewide discount, because bundling reframes the decision around perceived added value rather than pure price reduction.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Bundling and Average Order Value Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — bundling vs. flat discounts for order value

claim: In fintech onboarding, explicitly stating security/regulatory credentials (encryption standard, licensing body, insurance coverage) near account-creation forms reduces drop-off, because financial commitment carries higher perceived risk than typical ecommerce or SaaS signup.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Fintech Onboarding Trust Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — security credentials in fintech onboarding

options.label: Encryption/regulatory badges inline with signup form
Security credentials only in page footer

claim: Offering a low-friction 'try before you buy' path (demo booking, sample, or short assessment) converts skeptical high-consideration buyers better than a direct hard-sell CTA, particularly in categories with high switching cost or long-term commitment (education, fitness programs).
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'High-Consideration Purchase Funnel Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — low-friction try-before-you-buy for high-consideration purchases

options.label: Direct purchase CTA, no intermediate step

claim: The unity principle (framing the brand and customer as part of a shared identity or community, 'join us' rather than 'buy from us') increases affinity-driven conversion, particularly effective for fitness, education, and lifestyle communities built around shared identity.
paper: Cialdini, 'Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion', revised edition (2021) — unity principle
contextHeader: Conversion — unity/community framing

options.label: 'Join the community' framing over transactional framing

claim: For subscription products, prominently displaying an easy self-serve cancellation path (rather than requiring a support call) counterintuitively increases signup conversion, because it lowers the perceived commitment risk of trying the product.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Subscription Cancellation Friction Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — easy cancellation lowering signup friction

options.label: Self-serve cancellation mentioned near signup CTA

claim: Displaying a clear, simple refund/return policy summary (not buried in legal text) at the point of purchase reduces pre-purchase anxiety and measurably increases completed purchases in ecommerce, especially for higher-priced or unfamiliar-brand items.
paper: Baymard Institute, 'Return Policy and Purchase Confidence Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — visible return policy and purchase confidence

options.label: Plain-language return policy summary near CTA
Return policy link only in footer

claim: Urgency framing (limited-time discounts, flash sales) is more effective for low-consideration, low-price impulse categories (food, fast fashion) than for high-consideration categories (fintech, B2B software), where urgency can instead trigger suspicion and reduce trust.
paper: ConversionXL (CXL), 'Urgency Messaging Effectiveness by Product Category'
contextHeader: Conversion — urgency effectiveness varies by consideration level

options.label: No urgency framing for high-consideration categories

claim: Luxury and premium-positioned offers convert better with restraint-signaling scarcity (limited edition, made-to-order, waitlist access) than with discount-driven urgency, because discounting can erode the premium price anchor and perceived exclusivity.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Luxury Ecommerce Conversion Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — exclusivity framing over discounting for luxury

claim: Gamified progress mechanics (streaks, completion percentages, badges) increase conversion to sustained engagement in fitness and education products by leveraging the same completion-motivation documented in goal-gradient research, where motivation increases as perceived proximity to a goal increases.
paper: Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng, 'The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention' (Journal of Marketing Research, 2006)
contextHeader: Conversion — goal-gradient effect and gamified progress

claim: Displaying a clear comparison table against competitors or 'the old way' increases conversion for challenger brands and new entrants, because it explicitly frames the decision as a superior alternative rather than requiring the visitor to construct the comparison themselves.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Comparison Table Conversion Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — competitor comparison tables for challenger brands

options.label: Explicit feature comparison table vs. alternatives
No direct comparison, features stand alone

claim: A visible money-quantified guarantee ('get $X back if not satisfied' rather than vague 'satisfaction guaranteed') increases perceived seriousness of the guarantee and modestly increases conversion versus unquantified guarantee language.
paper: ConversionXL (CXL), 'Guarantee Framing Research'
contextHeader: Conversion — quantified vs. vague guarantee language

claim: Fitts's Law predicts that the time to acquire a target is a function of its distance and size — larger, closer interactive elements are selected faster and with fewer errors, which is why primary CTAs benefit from generous size and proximity to the user's likely focal point.
paper: Fitts, 'The Information Capacity of the Human Motor System in Controlling the Amplitude of Movement' (Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1954)
contextHeader: Layout — Fitts's Law and CTA size/placement

options.label: Large CTA positioned near the content that motivates it

claim: Hick's Law predicts that decision time increases logarithmically with the number of choices presented — navigation menus and option sets with fewer, well-organized choices are processed faster than long flat lists of options.
paper: Hick, 'On the Rate of Gain of Information' (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1952); Hyman, 1953
contextHeader: Layout — Hick's Law and navigation choice count

options.label: Grouped navigation with few top-level categories
Flat list of many navigation items

claim: Miller's Law (the '7±2 rule') suggests that working memory can hold roughly 5-9 discrete items at once, which is why grouping navigation items, form fields, or pricing tiers into chunks of this size (or fewer) reduces cognitive load versus longer ungrouped lists.
paper: Miller, 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information' (Psychological Review, 1956)
contextHeader: Layout — Miller's Law and chunking of navigation/options

options.label: Navigation/options chunked into small groups of 5-7

claim: The serial position effect predicts that items placed first (primacy) or last (recency) in a list or navigation menu are recalled and noticed more than items placed in the middle, which has implications for ordering pricing tiers, nav items, and feature lists.
paper: Murdock, 'The Serial Position Effect of Free Recall' (Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1962)
contextHeader: Layout — serial position effect in list/nav ordering

options.label: Most important items placed first and last in the list

claim: Eye-tracking research shows web users scan pages in an F-shaped or Z-shaped pattern depending on content density — text-heavy pages produce F-shaped scanning (heavy left-side and top attention), while sparser, more visual layouts produce Z-shaped scanning across the whole page.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'F-Shaped Pattern For Reading Web Content' (eye-tracking research)
contextHeader: Layout — F-pattern and Z-pattern scanning behavior

options.label: F-pattern layout for text-heavy content pages
Z-pattern layout for sparse, visual hero sections

claim: Visual hierarchy created through size, weight, and whitespace differences (rather than color alone) allows users to correctly identify a page's primary action within milliseconds, and pages lacking clear hierarchy show measurably slower task completion.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Visual Hierarchy in UX Design'
contextHeader: Layout — visual hierarchy via size/weight/whitespace

options.label: Strong size/weight contrast between primary and secondary elements

claim: Generous whitespace (negative space) around key content increases perceived premium quality and comprehension, while dense, low-whitespace layouts are perceived as lower-cost or lower-quality even when the underlying content is identical.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'The Role of Whitespace in UX Design'
contextHeader: Layout — whitespace and perceived quality

options.label: Generous whitespace, fewer elements per viewport
Dense layout, many elements per viewport

claim: Above-the-fold placement of key information still measurably affects engagement even though users do scroll — content immediately visible on load receives disproportionately more attention and time than content requiring a scroll, particularly on first visit.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Scrolling and Attention' (eye-tracking research)
contextHeader: Layout — above-the-fold attention weighting

options.label: Core value proposition fully visible without scrolling
Core message revealed after initial scroll

claim: Card-based layouts (discrete bounded content blocks) improve scanability and perceived organization for heterogeneous content (products, articles, features) compared to undifferentiated flowing text, because visual boundaries help users parse where one item ends and another begins.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Cards in UX Design'
contextHeader: Layout — card-based grouping for heterogeneous content

claim: A persistent, sticky navigation bar reduces the effort needed to switch sections and is preferred by users for long-scrolling or content-heavy pages, but on short pages it can consume valuable vertical space without a corresponding usability benefit.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Sticky Navigation Usability'
contextHeader: Layout — sticky navigation for long-scrolling pages

options.label: Sticky nav bar for long/content-heavy pages

claim: Breaking long forms into logical grouped sections with clear section headers reduces perceived effort and abandonment compared to a single undifferentiated wall of fields, even when the total number of fields is unchanged.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Form Design Guidelines'
contextHeader: Layout — grouped form sections and perceived effort

claim: Consistent grid alignment across a page (elements snapped to a shared column/baseline grid) is rated as more professional and 'polished' in usability testing than layouts with inconsistent or ad-hoc alignment, independent of the specific content shown.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Grid Systems in Web Design'
contextHeader: Layout — grid alignment and perceived polish

options.label: Strict shared grid alignment across sections

claim: Placing the most important navigation items or actions on the left side of a horizontal nav bar benefits left-to-right reading cultures because of the primacy of early-scanned positions, consistent with F-pattern scanning research.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'F-Shaped Pattern For Reading Web Content' — nav-order inference
contextHeader: Layout — left-weighted navigation for LTR reading patterns

options.label: Most important nav items positioned leftmost
Most important nav items positioned rightmost (near account/CTA)

claim: A single-column layout for primary content (rather than multi-column) is easier to scan and complete on mobile and reduces the risk of a user losing their place, which is why responsive form and checkout layouts collapse to a single column on small viewports.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Mobile Usability Guidelines'
contextHeader: Layout — single-column layouts for mobile forms/checkout

options.label: Retained multi-column layout on small viewports

claim: Proximity grouping (related elements placed closer together, unrelated elements separated by greater whitespace) is one of the strongest and most reliable Gestalt cues for helping users infer which controls act on which content, without needing explicit labels or borders.
paper: Wertheimer, Gestalt principles of perceptual organization (1923); applied to UI by Nielsen Norman Group
contextHeader: Layout — Gestalt proximity grouping

options.label: Related controls tightly grouped by proximity
Evenly spaced controls regardless of relation

claim: Similarity grouping (shared color, shape, or size signaling that items belong to the same category) helps users parse a page's structure faster than relying on position alone, and is why consistent card styling across a product grid speeds recognition of item type.
paper: Wertheimer, Gestalt principles of perceptual organization (1923); applied to UI by Nielsen Norman Group
contextHeader: Layout — Gestalt similarity grouping

options.label: Consistent visual styling across same-category items
Varied styling per item for visual interest

claim: Placing pricing information directly adjacent to the feature list it corresponds to reduces the memory burden of comparing price against value, versus separating pricing tables from feature explanations on different sections or pages.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Pricing Page Design Patterns'
contextHeader: Layout — pricing proximity to corresponding features

options.label: Price shown inline with its feature list
Price and features shown in separate sections

claim: Hero sections that pair a clear headline with a single supporting image or product visual are processed faster and rated as clearer than hero sections with multiple competing visual elements (carousels, multiple simultaneous images).
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Homepage and Hero Section Usability Research'
contextHeader: Layout — single-focus hero sections vs. carousels

claim: Table-based data display (rows and columns with aligned values) is scanned and compared significantly faster by users than the same data presented as repeated prose paragraphs, particularly for pricing, specs, or numeric comparisons.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Data Table Usability Research'
contextHeader: Layout — tabular display for comparable numeric data

options.label: Prose-style description of the same data

claim: Sidebar navigation with persistent visibility of the full site/app structure improves task efficiency for content-heavy or tool-heavy products with many sections, but adds visual complexity that can overwhelm first-time visitors on marketing-oriented pages.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Sidebar vs. Top Navigation Research'
contextHeader: Layout — sidebar navigation for tool-heavy products

options.label: Persistent sidebar nav for app/dashboard sections
Simple top nav for marketing-facing pages

claim: For senior audiences, larger touch/click targets and increased spacing between interactive elements reduce mis-clicks caused by age-related declines in fine motor precision, an effect consistent with Fitts's Law predictions at reduced motor accuracy.
paper: Fitts's Law (Fitts, 1954) applied to age-related motor precision — Nielsen Norman Group corroboration
contextHeader: Layout — larger targets and spacing for senior motor precision

options.label: Larger targets with generous spacing for senior-facing flows
Standard target sizing, no senior-specific adjustment

claim: Long-form landing pages that follow a logical narrative sequence (problem, solution, proof, offer) outperform pages with the same content presented in a non-sequential or scattered order, because the sequence mirrors the buyer's natural decision-making progression.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Landing Page Narrative Structure Research'
contextHeader: Layout — narrative sequencing in long-form landing pages

claim: For children's interfaces, simplified layouts with fewer simultaneous choices and larger, more clearly bounded interactive zones reduce task failure, consistent with both Hick's Law (fewer choices) and Fitts's Law (larger targets) but amplified by children's still-developing fine motor and executive function skills.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Designing for Children: Usability Research'
contextHeader: Layout — simplified layouts and large targets for children

options.label: Dense, adult-style layout with many small controls

claim: A visible, consistent footer with organized link categories (rather than a single flat list) improves findability of secondary information (legal, support, company info) and is where users predictably look when they cannot find something elsewhere on the page.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Footer Design Guidelines'
contextHeader: Layout — organized footer categories for findability

options.label: Footer organized into labeled link categories
Single flat list of footer links

claim: Z-pattern layouts (diagonal visual flow from top-left to bottom-right) are effective for sparse marketing pages with a clear single call-to-action, guiding the eye naturally from logo/headline through supporting visual to the CTA in the bottom-right.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Visual Flow Patterns in Web Design'
contextHeader: Layout — Z-pattern visual flow for sparse marketing pages

options.label: Z-pattern layout guiding eye toward bottom-right CTA

claim: Excessive nested navigation (three or more menu levels deep) significantly increases the likelihood a user abandons a task before finding what they need, compared to flatter information architectures with the same total content volume.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Information Architecture and Navigation Depth Research'
contextHeader: Layout — navigation depth and task abandonment

options.label: Flat IA, two levels of navigation depth max

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 between normal-size text and its background (3:1 for large text 18pt+/14pt bold+), below which text is considered inaccessible to users with low vision or color vision deficiencies.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
contextHeader: Accessibility — WCAG minimum text contrast ratio

claim: WCAG 2.1 recommends touch targets be at least 44x44 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.2 formalizes 24x24px as the AA minimum, with 44x44px recommended), since smaller targets significantly increase mis-tap rates for users with motor impairments or larger fingers.
paper: WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum); WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)
contextHeader: Accessibility — minimum touch target size

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that functionality triggered by motion-based interaction (device shake, pointer gesture) also be operable through conventional UI controls, and that animation triggered by interaction can be disabled unless essential, protecting users with motor or vestibular conditions.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
contextHeader: Accessibility — user control over interaction-triggered animation

options.label: Animation always enabled regardless of user preference

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that color not be the sole visual means of conveying information (e.g. error states, required fields, status indicators) because color-blind users and users with certain low-vision conditions cannot reliably distinguish hue-only signals.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color
contextHeader: Accessibility — color not the sole information signal

options.label: Icon/text label paired with color for status states

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires visible focus indicators for all keyboard-operable interface elements, since keyboard-only users (including many users with motor impairments) rely entirely on focus visibility to know where they are on the page.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible
contextHeader: Accessibility — visible keyboard focus indicators

options.label: High-contrast visible focus ring on all interactive elements
Default focus outline removed without replacement

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality, which requires layouts to use relative units and avoid fixed-height containers that clip enlarged text.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text
contextHeader: Accessibility — resizable text up to 200%

options.label: Fixed-pixel layout that may clip at 200% zoom

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that all functionality be operable through a keyboard alone, without requiring specific timing for individual keystrokes, since many users with motor impairments cannot use a pointing device at all.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 2.1.1 Keyboard
contextHeader: Accessibility — full keyboard operability

options.label: All interactive elements reachable and operable via keyboard
Some interactions require a pointing device

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that images convey their purpose through text alternatives (alt text) so that screen reader users receive equivalent information to sighted users viewing the image.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.1.1 Non-text Content
contextHeader: Accessibility — text alternatives for images

options.label: Descriptive alt text on all meaningful images

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that content and functionality not rely on a specific device orientation (portrait or landscape only) unless essential, since some users have devices fixed in a particular orientation due to mounting or motor constraints.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.3.4 Orientation
contextHeader: Accessibility — orientation-independent layouts

options.label: Layout adapts to both portrait and landscape

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that content flashing more than three times per second be avoided entirely, since rapid flashing can trigger seizures in users with photosensitive epilepsy — this is one of the few WCAG criteria with a direct physical safety implication.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold
contextHeader: Accessibility — seizure-safe flash-rate limits

options.label: No content flashes more than 3 times per second

claim: For older adults, accessibility accommodations (larger text, higher contrast, larger touch targets) often overlap directly with WCAG AA requirements, meaning designing to WCAG AA as a baseline also substantially improves usability for the senior segment specifically, not just users with permanent disabilities.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Senior Citizens and Web Usability' — cross-referenced with WCAG 2.1 AA criteria
contextHeader: Accessibility — WCAG AA baseline benefits older adults broadly

options.label: WCAG AA compliance treated as a senior-usability baseline
No specific accommodation beyond minimum legal requirement

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that form fields have programmatically associated labels (not placeholder text alone), since placeholder-only labels disappear on input and are not reliably exposed to assistive technology in the same way as persistent labels.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (form labeling guidance); Success Criterion 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions
contextHeader: Accessibility — persistent form labels vs. placeholder-only

options.label: Persistent visible labels above/beside each field
Placeholder text used as the only label

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that users be able to pause, stop, or hide any moving, blinking, or auto-updating content that starts automatically and lasts more than five seconds, since continuously moving content can distract users with attention-related or cognitive disabilities.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide
contextHeader: Accessibility — user control over auto-playing moving content

options.label: Auto-rotating/moving content includes a pause control
Auto-playing content with no pause control

claim: For neurodivergent users (including many with ADHD or autism spectrum conditions), reduced visual clutter, predictable layout patterns, and minimized unexpected motion measurably reduce cognitive load and task abandonment, even though this is not captured by a single specific WCAG criterion.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Designing for Neurodiversity' — inference from cognitive accessibility research
contextHeader: Accessibility — reduced clutter and predictability for neurodivergent users

options.label: Predictable layout with minimal unexpected motion/clutter

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio for the visual boundaries of user interface components (buttons, input borders, focus indicators) against adjacent colors, distinct from the 4.5:1 requirement for text, since low-contrast component boundaries are hard to perceive for low-vision users even when text within them is legible.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast
contextHeader: Accessibility — minimum contrast for UI component boundaries

claim: WCAG 2.1 requires that error messages identify the specific field in error and describe the error in text, rather than relying on a generic error state or color alone, so that screen reader users and users with cognitive disabilities can understand and correct the problem.
paper: WCAG 2.1, Success Criterion 3.3.1 Error Identification
contextHeader: Accessibility — specific, text-based error identification

options.label: Field-specific text error messages, not color alone

claim: UI transition animations in the roughly 200-500ms range are perceived as responsive and smooth; animations shorter than this feel imperceptible or abrupt, while animations longer than this feel sluggish and begin to actively slow down perceived task completion.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Animation Duration and Perceived Performance'; commonly-cited motion-design duration range
contextHeader: Motion — optimal UI transition duration range

claim: Motion that triggers vestibular disorder symptoms (large-scale parallax, zooming, or simulated 3D movement) can cause real physical discomfort (dizziness, nausea) for a meaningful subset of users, which is the underlying reason the prefers-reduced-motion media query exists and should be respected.
paper: W3C, prefers-reduced-motion specification rationale; cross-referenced with WCAG 2.1 SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
contextHeader: Motion — vestibular triggers and prefers-reduced-motion

options.label: Large-scale motion disabled when prefers-reduced-motion is set
Motion effects run regardless of user preference

claim: Loading animations (spinners, skeleton screens, progress indicators) improve perceived performance and reduce user-reported frustration during wait times, even when they do not change the actual load time, because they signal that the system is working rather than frozen.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable'
contextHeader: Motion — loading indicators and perceived performance

claim: Easing curves that mimic natural physical deceleration (ease-out) are perceived as smoother and more polished than linear or purely mechanical motion, because they mirror how physical objects move in the real world and match users' intuitive expectations.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Motion Design Principles for UX'
contextHeader: Motion — natural easing curves vs. linear motion

claim: Micro-interactions (small animated responses to user actions like a button press or toggle switch) provide immediate feedback that confirms an action registered, which reduces repeated/duplicate clicks caused by uncertainty about whether the first click worked.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Response Time Limits and Perceived System Feedback'
contextHeader: Motion — micro-interaction feedback and duplicate-click prevention

options.label: Immediate micro-animation on every interactive action

claim: Excessive or gratuitous animation on marketing pages (elements sliding, bouncing, or fading on every scroll trigger) can reduce perceived credibility for B2B and financial audiences, who associate restrained motion with seriousness and heavy scroll-triggered animation with lower-trust or less mature products.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Motion Design Principles for UX' — B2B credibility inference
contextHeader: Motion — restrained motion and B2B/financial credibility

options.label: Heavy scroll-triggered animation on most elements

claim: For gaming and youth-oriented entertainment products, energetic, elastic, or bouncy motion (overshoot easing) is associated with playfulness and fun and is preferred by younger audiences over the restrained, minimal-overshoot motion favored in professional/enterprise contexts.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Motion Design Principles for UX' — audience-preference inference
contextHeader: Motion — bouncy overshoot easing for playful/youth contexts

claim: Page transition animations that maintain spatial continuity (elements appearing to move from their prior position to their new one, rather than abruptly cutting) help users maintain a mental model of where content came from and reduce reported disorientation, particularly in multi-step flows.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Motion Design Principles for UX'
contextHeader: Motion — spatial continuity in page/step transitions

options.label: Transitions preserve spatial continuity between steps
Hard cut between pages/steps, no transition

claim: Autoplaying background video or large-scale motion on a hero section increases initial visual interest but can slow perceived page load and increase cognitive load for users trying to read accompanying text, creating a trade-off between visual energy and message clarity.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Autoplay Video and Motion in Hero Sections'
contextHeader: Motion — autoplay hero motion vs. message clarity trade-off

options.label: Subtle autoplay background motion behind text

claim: Staggered entrance animations (list or grid items appearing in sequence rather than simultaneously) are perceived as more polished and help direct attention item-by-item, but excessive stagger delay across long lists can make the interface feel slow to fully render.
paper: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Motion Design Principles for UX'
contextHeader: Motion — staggered entrance animation for lists/grids

options.label: All items appear simultaneously, no stagger
